Repository: re-cinq/HALEngine
Ticket: #37 Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema

You are editing files in a git repository, mid-way through a ticket that
is already defined by RED acceptance tests. You perform exactly ONE
red-green-refactor round and then stop. Not two. Not "while I'm here".

The ticket's branch is checked out with write access at /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/5e59bce86f07/workspace/target.
Run every command from inside it (`cd /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/5e59bce86f07/workspace/target` first). The ticket
is at `/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/5e59bce86f07/workspace/ticket.md`: read it before anything else. Pass `repo` (the
owner/name your task names above) on every `lore_*` call: the gateway has
no checkout to detect it from.

START by reading `.lore/dod.md` on this branch. Its "Done when these pass"
list is the bar; its Facets checklist is where the last round got to. It
names the strategy, the
acceptance tests that define done, and the facets expected. It is the
brief; the ticket below is the context.

RUN ONLY THE TEST YOU WRITE THIS ROUND, by its file, from the package
that owns it, with a deadline — for example `cd <package> && timeout 300 npx
vitest run <file>`. Never run the acceptance tests `.lore/dod.md` lists, nor a
directory that holds them: CI is the judge of this branch, runs them on
every push, and tells you where they stand. Read that from
`/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/5e59bce86f07/workspace/round-brief.md` when it exists, or ask `lore_get_ci_failures`
— not from your memory, and not from what `.lore/dod.md` predicted. Not
the repository's full suite either, not lint, not the typechecker, not
the formatter. The pod's Bash hook refuses an acceptance test by name and
a runner given no test file.

If this pod cannot run your test — the command that runs it (`java`, `mvn`,
`gradle`, `go`, `cargo`, `dotnet`) is not found, or a wrapper such as
`./mvnw` reports no `JAVA_HOME` — do not look for it and do not install
it: no `sudo`, no `apt`, no `find /`, no download. Do the round from the
code, the tests and CI's verdict, commit and push; CI judges the push,
and a red build comes back to the next round as its brief. Say in your
final message that the round ran no tests here.

YOUR ROUND is the `tdd-loop` skill's three phases, in order, no steps
skipped: one failing test for the smallest facet that moves an acceptance
test closer to green, then the least code that passes it, then refactor
with the bar green. Never edit an acceptance test to make it pass — if an
acceptance test is wrong, stop and say so; that is a failed round.

Under `parallel-change`, all of this happens in the NEW module: leave the
old code alone and working until the acceptance tests are green, and make
the caller switch its own round. Under `characterize`, the
characterization tests are part of the green bar you must keep — a
refactor that reddens them is a behaviour change. Under `mechanical`,
there is no red phase at all: perform the exact edits its Facets
record and commit; the EXISTING tests `.lore/dod.md` names are CI's to
run, and its verdict says whether they stayed green. The diff is the
deliverable, and a round that invents a new test for it has left the
strategy.

Never add a test whose assertion subject is the repo's own source text —
readFileSync of a src/ or test file, a regex over another test,
counting a literal across files. That pins prose, not behaviour: where
prose must agree with a value, make the prose compute the value instead.

TRACEABILITY:
- Each test validates a statement in a spec or ADR. Add the inline
  parenthetical on that statement in the repository's established form —
  `Statement. ([validated by name](path/to/test.ts#L42))`. Inserting a
  test shifts every #Lnn link below it: when the repository has
  `scripts/spec-links/reanchor.mjs`, run
  `node scripts/spec-links/reanchor.mjs` from the repository root after
  the formatter — it moves each link to its test's current line, by test
  title, and prints the links it could not map, which you fix by hand.
  Without it, re-verify every existing #Lnn link on the statements you
  touch yourself.
- Stamp the test's spec anchor (the "specs/<path>#<ordinal>" it
  validates) so the repo's tests.list surfaces it as the descriptor's
  `spec` field and the VALIDATED_BY link is established automatically —
  see `.lore/test-commands.yml` for how this repo exposes descriptors.

- If this round completes what a `specs/<name>/spec.md` describes, update
  that spec's `| Status |` header row in the same branch (Draft ->
  Implemented/Shipped) so the status never lags the code.

BEFORE YOU EDIT A SYMBOL, ask the graph which tests already cover it:
`lore-query-trace` with `tests_covering` set to the file you are about to
change, and `ranges` as `start-end` when you know the span. The rows name
test FILES, because coverage is recorded per file, and they describe the
repository as main last projected it.

Main is the right coordinate for this question: a REGRESSION is by
definition a test that existed before your branch. That list is what tells
a red test apart from one. When CI's verdict on your last push names a
red test you did not write and the acceptance list does not hold, it is
a regression YOU caused — stop, fix the
code, and never "fix" the test. Say in your final message how many red
tests were yours and how many were regressions.

RULES:
- Do not fix unrelated smells you notice. Name them in your final message;
  act on none of them.
- Keep `.lore/dod.md` current: TICK the box of the facet you closed
  (`- [ ]` becomes `- [x]`) and append any new facet you discovered as an
  unchecked one. It is a live checklist, not an append-only log, and the
  next round reads it to see where the ticket actually stands.
- Commit when the test YOU wrote is green. Acceptance tests may still be
  red — that is the ordinary state mid-ticket, and the next round takes
  the next facet.
- If `/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/5e59bce86f07/workspace/round-brief.md` exists, read it before `.lore/dod.md`. Its
  `The previous round reported` section is where the last round stopped.
  Its `CI reported failures` section is the verdict
  on the previous push, and it outranks `.lore/dod.md`: a red build means
  the ticket is NOT done, however many facets are ticked. Every finding
  it lists — each `path:line message` — is work this round owes before
  anything else. Fix ALL of them in this visit, format, push; there is no
  local re-run here that would show you the rest, and each finding you
  leave costs the ticket a pod and a CI cycle. Run 2a291314 spent two
  rounds reading a ticked dod.md and reporting "nothing left" under a
  verdict naming three lines; the guard sent it to repair each time. Do
  not re-run the whole build to find the failures; the section names them.

DELIVERY, NON-NEGOTIABLE — the next step runs in a DIFFERENT container:
- Before you commit, run the repository's FORMATTER over the files you
  changed (`npx prettier --write <files>`, `gofmt -w <files>`, whichever
  this repo uses) and nothing else from CI's checklist. Do NOT run the
  linter in this pod: CI runs it on every push, and here it does not
  fit — in this repository a two-file `eslint` peaks near 800 MB against
  a 1Gi pod, and runs 112256d9 and 62c1ca5e were OOM-killed on exactly
  that. A lint finding comes back as a red build naming the file and
  line, which the next round fixes with an editor.
- Do NOT typecheck here either. A green test is not a compiled build —
  vitest transpiles each file without checking types — but CI's build
  step is what proves it, and in this repository `tsc --noEmit` on
  `libs/shared` peaks near 950 MB against the 1Gi pod: run 2a291314's
  dod pod was OOM-killed on it. A type error comes back as a red build
  whose failed step and log tail name the file and line; the next
  round fixes it there. Read your imports and signatures twice instead.
- NEVER run a workspace build in this pod (`npm run build`, `tsc -b`, a
  `tsc` without `--noEmit`): tests resolve every workspace package from
  SOURCE, so nothing needs building for a test to see your change, and
  the build is the 950 MB step that OOM-killed run abac6ee9 while it
  rebuilt libs/shared for a test that never needed it.
- When the work is done, `git -C /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/5e59bce86f07/workspace/target add` what you changed and commit it with a
  short, factual message. Then `git -C /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/5e59bce86f07/workspace/target push origin HEAD`. The clone carries
  its own credentials, so a plain push authenticates; you need no token
  and must never look for one.
- Then bring the branch up to date with its base — `git fetch origin main`
  and merge `origin/main` in — and push again if that produced anything.
  A branch that cannot merge cleanly gets NO CI AT ALL: GitHub runs no
  workflow on a conflicted pull request, so the ticket parks on a build
  that will never start. Resolve any conflict now, favouring `origin/main`
  for anything this ticket did not write, and never by discarding your own
  work. This is why a nine-day-old branch stalled: 186 commits of drift,
  no checks, and a wait with nothing to wait for.
- Confirm it landed: `git status` must report the branch is not ahead of
  its upstream. An unpushed commit lives only in this container and
  dies with it — do NOT report success for one.
- If you genuinely changed nothing, say why — and read the result lines
  below before you choose one: "nothing left to write" and "I am stuck"
  are different endings here, and only the second is a failure.
- Do not open a pull request: you have no `gh` and no GitHub token. Lore
  opens the PR from the branch you push.

THE LAST LINE YOU PRINT is how the round ends. Print exactly one, on its
own line, as the final thing in your message. You are NOT deciding whether
the ticket is done — the build decides that, after your push. You are
reporting whether this round delivered anything.
- You committed and pushed a round:
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"success","extras":{"tdd_done":"<the facet you closed>","tdd_next":"<the facet the next round takes, or 'acceptance green'>"}}
  This is the ordinary outcome, whether or not acceptance tests remain
  red. CI reads the branch next and sends you back if there is more.
- You wrote nothing because there was nothing left to write — every facet
  in `.lore/dod.md` is closed, its acceptance tests pass, AND no
  `CI reported failures` section is in the round brief (a red verdict IS something
  left to write; fix its findings and report the line above instead):
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"success","extras":{"tdd_next":"acceptance green"}}
  SUCCESS, not failure. The branch is already pushed; the build judges it
  next, and a green one sends the ticket to review. Reporting failure for
  a round that found the work already done ENDS THE TICKET and strands its
  work on an open branch — which is exactly how run ae788c93 died with the
  implementation complete and all four facets checked off.
- You cannot name a next facet, or the bar will not go green: say exactly
  what blocks you, then:
  LORE_NODE_RESULT: {"outcome":"failed","extras":{"tdd_blocked":"<one line: what blocks you>"}}
  "This is hard" is not stuck; "there is no facet I can express as a test"
  is. Report failure when you are STUCK, never when you are FINISHED.

    Jest 30 instruments branch points jest 29 never saw, so every branch floor is
    read by a different instrument than the one that set it. Across src/ the branch
    count goes 240/350 covered to 332/473, while statements (665/842), functions
    (180/226) and lines (601/756) are identical to the unit - the same 385 tests,
    none added, none removed.

    so because its denominator grew: vertex 69.23 -> 74.64, mock 75 -> 78.57 and
    global 59.42 -> 64.82 rise, while orchestration 85.91 -> 80.85 and its tools
    57.14 -> 56.25 fall. Three floors tighten and two loosen, which is the finer
    instrument reading the same suite rather than coverage being lost.
    
    AGENTS.md gains the case, because the rule it states - a floor that moves down
    is a regression with the alarm switched off - is otherwise contradicted here
    with nothing to say why.

Author: vvondruska <2923801+vvondruska@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Mon Sep 14 09:17:22 2026 +0200

    release: 0.2.1, the first tokenless publish (#30)
    
    * build: delete the workflow that published once
    
    It did its single use: 0.2.0 exists, the trusted publisher is registered against
    publish.yml, the token is revoked and the secret is gone. What is left is a
    dispatchable job holding a publish step, guarded only by a version check that a
    future bump would walk straight past.
    
    Its reason for existing was that a trusted publisher cannot be registered
    against a name the registry has never seen. That is no longer true of this name,
    and cannot become true again.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01LwoztdBKudtfu3JJkfamWx
    
    * release: 0.2.1, the first tokenless publish
    
    Identical to 0.2.0 - same files, same code. It exists to prove that a release
    reaches the registry with no credential stored in the repository: 0.2.0 could
    only be published with a token, because a trusted publisher cannot be registered
    against a name the registry has never seen, and this is the first version
    released through that publisher instead.
    
    The readme said the first release had not happened yet. It has, and that
    sentence is the npm front page, so it now describes how versions are published
    rather than promising one.

Author: vvondruska <vondruska.vaclav@gmail.com>
Date:   Sun Sep 13 14:16:30 2026 +0200

    build: override the uuid gaxios cannot move off (#19)
    
    npm audit reported two moderate advisories that are one root: gaxios 6
    pins uuid to ^9, and the advisory is fixed in 11.1.1, so the nested copy
    cannot be patched where it sits. Escaping it means leaving gaxios 6,
    which means leaving google-auth-library 9, which the Vertex SDK
    requires - including 1.12.0, the newest version this range allows. npm
    audit fix does not clear it either; it rewrites the lockfile and exits 1
    with both advisories intact.
    
    An override forces uuid to ^11.1.1 under gaxios alone. uuid 11 still
    ships a CommonJS entry point, which gaxios needs because it requires
    rather than imports.
    
    The exposure was never real - gaxios calls v4() with no buffer, and the
    advisory covers v3, v5 and v6 when one is supplied - and the gate fails
    only at high and above. The tree is now at zero so the next advisory is
    visible rather than filed behind standing noise.

Author: vvondruska <vaclav@re-cinq.com>
Date:   Fri Sep 11 23:48:45 2026 +0200

    fix: stop the citation tool guessing, and hold three gates to their claims
    
    Findings from an adversarial review of the last twelve commits. The
    first one is the serious one, and it had already fired.
    
    check-spec-anchor-names resolved a duplicated test name by proximity.
    The nearest declaration is the one the author meant only while the shift
    is smaller than half the gap between the duplicates; past that it rewrites
    the spec to cite the wrong test and every gate then reports clean. The
    repository already contained the trigger - chats.test.ts declared
    "answers 404 for a chat that does not exist" twice, once for GET and once
    for POST, and both were cited. Renaming the POST test made --fix collapse
    the POST citation onto the GET declaration, in this working tree, before
    anyone noticed.
    
    Proximity resolution is gone. A name matching two declarations is now
    reported whether or not the line currently agrees - the old code
    short-circuited on a matching line, so while the lines happened to be
    right nothing ever said the name identified two tests - and --fix refuses
    to touch it. The two tests were renamed apart. A name carrying a bracket
    is refused rather than written into a markdown label it would terminate,
    which would have made the citation vanish from this gate, from
    check-spec-links and from the coverage job at once.
    
    smoke.sh could not run under bash 3.2, which is /bin/bash on macOS: "${peers[@]}"
    on an empty array is an unbound variable under set -u. AGENTS.md tells a
    maintainer to run this locally before a release and this repository's
    platform is darwin, so the local gate was broken for everyone who has one.
    The RETURN trap also leaked the work directory whenever set -u or the
    watchdog exited past it; it is an EXIT trap over an accumulating list now.
    
    The late-error listener had no test at all, and removing it entirely left
    321 tests green. It also reported a cleanly refused start as a running
    server's error, because stop() left it attached: an operator alerting on
    that category got paged for something that was correctly rejected and
    handed back. The listener is now removed before each bind attempt.
    Writing the test found the other half: removing it in stop() as well -
    which the first draft did - reintroduces the fatal path, because an error
    arriving after stop then has no handler. It stays attached.
    
    check-audit's cycle test asserted the absence of a substring, so deleting
    the cycle guard kept it green: the script died of a stack overflow and the
    trace contained no "unknown:" either. It asserts the exit status and both
    expected findings now, and dedupe has a diamond case - each fails when its
    guard is removed.
    
    check-doc-regions read one of CommonMark's fence spellings, unindented,
    while its spec claimed it reads fenced blocks. An indented fence in a
    numbered list - the ordinary way a guide writes a step - was invisible,
    and so was a tilde fence. check-doc-paths claimed every backticked
    repository path and checked four prefixes; it checks ten now, and the two
    paths that legitimately do not resolve are named in an allowlist with
    their reasons rather than the pattern being narrowed around them. 147
    paths became 205.
    
    The per-path coverage floors were set at 70 under a comment claiming all
    four sat well above it. Vertex's branches were 69.23 - below it - which is
    why that one had been quietly lowered to 65. Naming four paths had also
    exempted them from the global floor and handed each an 18-to-30 point
    regression budget the single global row never allowed. All five are set at
    measurement now, and src/orchestration/tools/ is named separately because
    a path floor is a prefix match and a regression in the tools registry
    otherwise hides inside the orchestration figure.
    
    prettier:check covered src/ only, so scripts/ drifted; the range had added
    a file into that hole. It covers {src,scripts,smoke}/**/*.ts now.

    build: cite tests by name, and derive the line from it
    
    A citation named a line, and a line is not what the author meant. Adding
    one import above a suite moves every test below it, so each citation
    lands on a different, still-valid declaration - the spec still reads as
    cited, pointing at the wrong test, and nothing notices. It happened four
    times on this branch alone, and every repair was by hand.
    
    repoint-spec-anchors cannot catch it: it compares against a baseline, and
    skips any spec whose anchor set differs from the base ref - which is
    precisely the spec being edited. The gate was green on this branch while
    validating none of the four specs under change.
    
    Citations now carry the test's name:
    
      ([validated by](../../src/x.test.ts#L209))
      ([validated by: refuses an empty-string id](../../src/x.test.ts#L209))
    
    The name travels with the citation, so the check needs no baseline. The
    line stays because both consumers index by it - the require-spec-link rule
    and the coverage job - and a citation carrying no line marks the WHOLE
    file covered rather than one test, which is the weakest reading available.
    Verified against the vendored parser both use: links are classified by
    path, and the label is free text, so nothing downstream reads what was
    added.
    
    check-spec-anchor-names holds each citation to the declaration it names
    and repoints the line from the name with --fix. Proved on the real defect:
    inserting a line at the top of chats.test.ts moved 24 citations, the check
    named every one with the line it should carry, and --fix repaired all 24
    with no hand editing. Restoring the file round-tripped them back.
    
    A name declared twice in one file resolves to the nearest declaration,
    because a stale citation is stale by a shift and the match a few lines
    away is the one meant; two equally distant candidates are reported rather
    than guessed at.
    
    Migration was the tool's own --fix over 302 existing citations. Eight
    tests, over committed fixtures. AGENTS.md § Spec Test Links documents the
    format and specs/hal-engine-doc-gates/spec.md carries the statements.

commit 573b50a9218a60b2580ac94dc17bee5b518b91bc
Author: vvondruska <vaclav@re-cinq.com>
Date:   Fri Sep 11 22:27:47 2026 +0200

    build: gate the three documentation rules nobody was enforcing
    
    Three rules this repository committed to and then kept by memory alone.
    Each was already broken at least once before anyone noticed.
    
    check-doc-paths resolves every backticked repository path in a document.
    A path in prose is a citation, and one nobody resolves rots in silence:
    the file moves, the sentence naming it stays, and the next reader follows
    it to nothing. 147 paths resolve across 21 documents today. Placeholders
    and globs name no single file and are skipped; a :line suffix is dropped,
    because which line a citation lands on is repoint-spec-anchors' question.
    
    check-spike-status requires every docs/spikes/ document to open with a
    status block. A spike records what somebody believed on the day they
    wrote it; served as documentation without that said out loud - and Lore
    does serve these - it reads as current design, which is how a superseded
    proposal becomes the thing somebody implements. A block buried below the
    head of the file fails too: a reader meets the body first.
    
    check-doc-regions refuses a non-EU region in anything a reader copies.
    `location` and `region` reach the vendor SDK unvalidated, so a US region
    in an example is a cross-border transfer somebody made by following the
    documentation. It reads fenced blocks and source files, not prose - a
    spec sentence recording that an example USED to name a US region is an
    account of a correction, and rewriting it would erase the record. The
    eu-/europe- prefix is a vendor naming convention rather than a legal
    test, which the spec says plainly: eu-west-2 is London.
    
    check-doc-blocks also gains the suite it never had, and a fence matcher
    that is no longer trivially escapable. It matched ```typescript exactly,
    so retagging a block ```ts - which renders identically and is already
    used elsewhere here - left the marker in place and stopped the block
    being compared. It now recognises ts, tsx, capitalisation and info
    strings, and reports an unclosed fence rather than comparing to the end
    of the file. Fifteen cases, including the retag that used to pass.
    
    All four are wired into package.json and run as their own CI steps, so a
    red run names the rule that broke. specs/hal-engine-doc-gates/spec.md
    carries the statements and cites each test.

Author: vvondruska <vaclav@re-cinq.com>
Date:   Fri Sep 11 15:53:51 2026 +0200

    build: publish from a v* tag with no stored token
    
    T011. A v* tag runs two jobs: everything CI already gates, re-run
    against the tagged commit, and then the publish.
    
    They are separate jobs so id-token: write is minted only after the gates
    pass - a tag points wherever its author chose, so a green run on main is
    not evidence about what is being released. The version guard runs in
    both, because the second time is the last gate before the one step here
    that cannot be undone.
    
    scripts/check-version.sh is a script rather than an inline step so it can
    run before the tag exists, which is the only time the answer is still
    useful. It rejects a prerelease tag outright: nothing passes --tag, so
    one would publish as latest.
    
    The pack-list guard checks the only place shipping a test is a fact
    rather than an intention. npm ci --ignore-scripts throughout, and
    --ignore-scripts on publish too, so what ships is the tree the build step
    produced rather than a second build of it.

    test: smoke-test the packed tarball in an empty consumer
    
    Nothing in this repository had ever installed the package from a
    tarball, so neither the exports map, nor files, nor the dependency list,
    nor the emitted .d.ts had been exercised the way a consumer exercises
    them. scripts/smoke.sh and the smoke/ fixture now do, as their own CI
    job; the release workflow will call the same script before npm publish.
    
    Two details are load-bearing rather than stylistic. The install happens
    outside the repository tree, because inside it Node and tsc walk up to
    this repo's own node_modules and every missing dependency resolves
    anyway - the check would pass on a package that fails for a real
    consumer. And everything installs in one npm install, because a later
    --no-save run prunes packages absent from package.json, silently
    removing the subject and turning the type check into a
    cannot-find-module false negative.
    
    The type half runs with skipLibCheck: false so the published .d.ts must
    compile on its own; that setting is what surfaced the @types defect the
    manifest commit fixed.
    
    Proven to catch what it exists to catch, not just to pass: reverting the
    @types move reproduces 8 tsc errors, and restoring the top-level Vertex
    import reproduces ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Both fail this script and
    nothing else in the suite.
    
    smoke/ is excluded from tsconfig.json and tsconfig.build.json the way
    example is - it compiles against the published package, not src/. It
    sits outside the jest roots and outside files, so it is neither tested
    in place nor published; npm pack --dry-run lists zero smoke files.

commit e4f93cae355dd2240c619a78f7ee74f815a8fdca
Author: vvondruska <vaclav@re-cinq.com>
Date:   Fri Sep 11 14:35:12 2026 +0200

    test: gate CI on a committed coverage floor
    
    AGENTS.md has long listed CI checks in its PR acceptance criteria, and
    ci.yml runs them, but nothing measured coverage - so the suite could
    thin out silently. jest.config.js now carries collectCoverageFrom and
    coverageThreshold, package.json a test:coverage script, and ci.yml's
    Test step calls it instead of npm test rather than running the suite
    twice. coverage/ was already gitignored.
    
    Measured with test files and providerTestSupport.ts excluded: 67.96%
    statements, 57.54% branches, 68% functions, 68.34% lines over 206 tests
    in 17 suites.
    
    The floor sits exactly at those numbers, not rounded down. Integer
    floors were tried first and measured to leave about a percent of slack:
    four untested lines appended to logger.ts passed the gate. At the exact
    baseline the same four lines fail it on all four metrics by name, and
    the gate goes green again when they are removed. A ratchet with slack in
    it is not a ratchet.
    
    Coverage is collected from src/ only. The scripts/ suites drive their
    subjects through spawnSync, so an instrumented .mjs reports zero however
    well it is tested, and a floor computed over those files would measure
    the harness rather than the code.
    
    Verified: typecheck, eslint, prettier, 206/206 tests under the new gate,
    build, and the spec gates.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01CyFimiuBEQXWWBktCx6gHE

commit 415b0a177f2c3e0196425fa1a62cd66671e6293b
Author: vvondruska <vaclav@re-cinq.com>
Date:   Fri Sep 11 14:33:49 2026 +0200

    build: publish as @re-cinq/hal-engine under Apache-2.0
    
    Takes the manifest from a private-repo application to a publishable
    package: scoped name, 0.2.0 for the ESM break, Apache-2.0 with a LICENSE
    file, repository, a single-root exports map, engines >=22 and
    publishConfig.access public. main and types are kept beside exports, as
    the reference implementation keeps them. bugs arrives with the
    vulnerability-disclosure task.
    
    The LICENSE body is the canonical Apache text taken verbatim from a copy
    in the tree and diffed against a second copy to confirm the two agree;
    only the appendix copyright line is ours.
    
    Type-checking the packed tarball in an empty project surfaced a real
    manifest defect: the emitted .d.ts files import express, http, stream
    and ws unconditionally - types/auth.d.ts and three files under
    transport/ - while every matching @types package sat in devDependencies.
    A consumer resolved the runtime and then failed to compile, with eight
    TS7016/TS2591/TS2307 errors. @types/express, @types/node and @types/ws
    move to dependencies; the same check now exits 0 with neither optional
    peer installed. The @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime reference in the
    emitted types is not the same problem - it is a typeof import() inside a
    function body, not public surface, and survives the peer being absent.
    
    engines >=22 is safe rather than assumed: both optional peers are
    CommonJS, so requireOptionalPeer's createRequire never needs Node's
    require(esm) support and its 22.12 floor.
    
    Renaming the package breaks every bare specifier, so the import and
    install lines in README.md, docs/getting-started.md and the providers
    spec move to the scoped name. Rewriting those documents is still the
    docs task's job; this only keeps the package name true.
    
    Verified: typecheck, eslint, prettier, 206/206 tests, build, and a
    packed tarball installed into an empty ESM project - runtime resolve and
    clean tsc with neither optional peer present.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit 1c9af89d9c10bf833908bcbb41f0dae60899a6d0
Author: vvondruska <vaclav@re-cinq.com>
Date:   Fri Sep 11 14:30:43 2026 +0200

    build: convert the package to ESM-only output
    
    Breaking: the package now publishes ESM only. A CommonJS consumer must
    move to `import`, or stay on the previous version. AGENTS.md § Breaking
    Changes requires the MINOR bump, which the manifest task carries.
    
    The six require() sites resolve two different ways, because they were
    doing two different jobs. The five in providerFactory.ts were a lazy
    loading boundary that never loaded anything lazily: src/index.ts
    statically re-exports all five provider factories, so importing the
    package root already pulled every provider module in. Measured before
    and after this commit, a bare root import of dist/ loads 38
    @google-cloud/vertexai modules and 0 @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime
    modules either way. They become static imports. The sixth, the AWS SDK
    in bedrockProvider.ts, is a real boundary around an optional peer and
    keeps it via createRequire(import.meta.url) - require() of an external
    CJS package, not of our own ESM. The next commit gives vertex the same
    treatment and takes that 38 to 0.
    
    That moves the prefer-polymorphism suppression's justification, so
    ADR-006 is rewritten rather than left asserting a loading boundary the
    factory no longer owns. The switch stays, now justified by the
    discriminated-union narrowing five differently-typed config arms need -
    the same premise the validateMessage entry already records.
    
    Jest runs as real ESM (--experimental-vm-modules, ts-jest useESM)
    rather than compiling the suite to CommonJS: an ESM-only package whose
    tests exercise CJS output would hide the failure class this conversion
    is about. The cost is three test files - ESM injects no `jest` global,
    so they import it from @jest/globals, and jest.mock does not hoist, so
    the vertex suite uses unstable_mockModule with a dynamic import. Those
    imports shift line numbers, so spec anchors are repointed with
    scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs.
    
    ts-node is replaced by tsx: `--import ts-node/esm` does not rewrite
    `./x.js` to `./x.ts` on Node 24 and the example server failed to
    resolve src/index.js. Verified by booting it and getting 200 from
    /api/health. ts-node had no other dependent - ts-jest does not need it.
    
    The add-a-provider recipe's steps 2 and 3 wrote extensionless relative
    imports, which do not resolve under NodeNext ESM; both now carry .js.
    
    Verified: typecheck, eslint, prettier, 197/197 tests, build, and the
    spec gates.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Date:   Fri Sep 11 14:03:33 2026 +0200

    chore: initial commit
    
    HAL Engine: a generic AI chat server framework with pluggable providers,
    tools, and transport. Imported from an internal working repository at its
    main branch, with cross-project references removed so the tree stands on
    its own.
    
    What the import changed, and nothing else:
    
    Prose that named sibling repositories now describes the thing itself -
    lint-rule rationale in eslint.config.mjs and eslint.config.backlog.mjs,
    the spec-tooling convention in AGENTS.md, the suppression reasoning in
    ADR-006, and the upstream-parser notes in the spec-status and
    spec-link-placement specs. The nine spec-status fixtures carry a generic
    issue slug. Header comments in check-spec-links.mjs and
    check-spec-status.mjs no longer name the upstream project.
    
    Kept deliberately, because the tooling needs them: the .lore manifest,
    the lore-ingest and lore-trace-impact workflows, the three issue
    templates, scripts/lore-*.mjs, and @re-cinq/eslint-plugin-re-lint with
    its rule ids.
    
    .gitignore gains the Claude Code entries. The source repo hid
    settings.local.json and skills/ in .git/info/exclude, which is per-clone
    and never travels, so a second contributor would have had their own
    absolute paths swept in by git add -A. worktrees/ joins them because
    Prettier reads those files.
    
    The issue-template contact link is gone rather than repointed; it
    carried an unsubstituted LORE_UI_DOMAIN placeholder that would have
    rendered as a broken link, and an external contributor has no dashboard
    to visit. That slot is where a security-disclosure link belongs.
    
    LORE_INGEST_URL now resolves from a secret first and falls back to the
    existing repository variables, and no longer reaches the log: the two
    curl-failure messages name the endpoint generically, and each of the
    four steps masks the value explicitly, because Actions masks secrets
    automatically but not variables.
    
    Verified: typecheck, eslint, prettier, 197/197 tests, build, the spec
    link and status gates, and the traceability backlog report.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
